content: Salmeterol, when used by patients with asthma, has been associated with an increased risk of severe or fatal asthma-related complications. This was observed in a large clinical study where more asthma-related deaths occurred in patients using salmeterol compared to those who did not. If you have asthma, salmeterol should only be prescribed if other medications have failed to control your symptoms or if your asthma is so severe that it requires two medications for adequate management. Salmeterol should never be the first or sole medication used to treat asthma. It is not appropriate for use in cases of rapidly worsening asthma. Inform your doctor if you have experienced frequent severe asthma attacks or if you have ever been hospitalized due to asthma symptoms. If you notice any of the following signs of worsening asthma, contact your doctor immediately: Your short-acting inhaler is less effective than before. You need to use more puffs or use your short-acting inhaler more frequently than usual. You require four or more puffs of your short-acting inhaler daily for two or more consecutive days. You use more than one canister (200 inhalations) of your short-acting inhaler within an 8-week period. Your peak-flow meter readings indicate worsening breathing problems. You require emergency room treatment for asthma. Your symptoms fail to improve after one week of regular salmeterol use or worsen at any point during treatment. Discuss the risks of using salmeterol with your doctor. You will receive a Medication Guide from your doctor or pharmacist when starting salmeterol and with each prescription refill. Read this guide carefully and ask any questions you may have. Additional information can be found on the FDA or manufacturer’s website. Salmeterol is prescribed to alleviate wheezing, shortness of breath, and breathing difficulties caused by asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema. It is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm. Salmeterol belongs to a class of drugs called long-acting beta agonists (LABAs) and works by relaxing and opening the airways in the lungs, making breathing easier. Salmeterol is available as a dry powder for oral inhalation using a specially designed inhaler. For asthma or COPD, it is typically used twice daily, once in the morning and once in the evening, approximately 12 hours apart. It should be used at the same times each day. For exercise-induced breathing difficulties, it is usually taken at least 30 minutes before exercise, but not more than once every 12 hours. If you are already using salmeterol twice daily, do not take an additional dose before exercising. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully and use salmeterol exactly as directed. Do not use more or less of the medication or use it more frequently than prescribed. Consult your doctor about how to use other asthma medications during your salmeterol treatment. If you are taking a corticosteroid, your doctor will likely advise you to continue its use as before. If you were using a short-acting beta agonist inhaler like albuterol regularly, your doctor may instruct you to stop regular use but continue using it for sudden asthma symptoms. Do not alter your medication regimen without consulting your doctor. Salmeterol is not intended for use during acute asthma or COPD attacks. Your doctor will prescribe a short-acting inhaler for such emergencies. While salmeterol helps control symptoms of asthma and other lung diseases, it does not cure them. Do not stop using salmeterol without consulting your doctor, as sudden discontinuation may worsen your symptoms. Before using the salmeterol inhaler for the first time, ask your doctor, pharmacist, or respiratory therapist to demonstrate its use. Practice using the inhaler under their supervision. Follow these steps to use the inhaler: 1. If using a new inhaler, remove it from the box and foil wrapper. Write the date you opened the pouch and the replacement date (6 weeks later) on the inhaler label. 2. Hold the inhaler in one hand and place your thumb on the thumbgrip. Push your thumb away from you until the mouthpiece appears and locks into position. 3. Hold the inhaler horizontally with the mouthpiece facing you. Slide the lever away from you until it clicks, preparing a dose for inhalation. The dose counter will decrease by one. Avoid wasting doses by mishandling the lever or tilting the inhaler. 4. Exhale fully, keeping the inhaler level and away from your mouth. 5. Place the mouthpiece to your lips and inhale quickly and deeply through the inhaler (not your nose). 6. Remove the inhaler from your mouth and hold your breath for 10 seconds or as long as comfortable. Exhale slowly. 7. You may taste or feel the salmeterol powder. If not, do not take another dose. 8. Slide the thumbgrip back toward you to close the inhaler. Do not exhale into the inhaler, disassemble it, or wash any part of it. Keep the inhaler dry and do not use it with a spacer. Salmeterol may be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using salmeterol, inform your doctor if you are allergic to salmeterol, milk protein, or any other substances. Notify your doctor if you are using another LABA, such as fluticasone-salmeterol (Advair) or formoterol (Foradil), as these should not be used concurrently with salmeterol. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Mention any beta blockers, diuretics, asthma or COPD medications, antidepressants, or monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) you are currently using or have recently discontinued. Your doctor may adjust your medication regimen or monitor you for side effects. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while using salmeterol, contact your doctor. Continue your normal diet unless otherwise instructed by your doctor. If you miss a dose, skip it and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Mild side effects of salmeterol may include uncontrollable shaking, headache, nervousness, dizziness, cough, nasal congestion, ear pain, pale skin, muscle pain or cramps, sore throat, flu-like symptoms, nausea, heartburn, tooth pain, dry mouth, mouth sores, red or irritated eyes, difficulty sleeping, or tingling in the hands or feet. Notify your doctor if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects may include coughing, wheezing, or chest tightness shortly after inhalation; rapid or irregular heartbeat; chest pain; rash; hives; swelling of the face, throat, or extremities; hoarseness; difficulty swallowing; or high-pitched breathing. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Report any unusual side effects to your doctor or the FDA MedWatch program. Store salmeterol in its original container, tightly sealed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Discard the inhaler 6 weeks after opening the foil wrapper or when the dose counter reads 0, whichever comes first. Consult your pharmacist for proper disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual has collapsed or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include seizures, chest pain, dizziness, fainting, blurred vision, rapid or irregular heartbeat, nervousness, headache, uncontrollable shaking, muscle cramps, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, or difficulty sleeping. Keep all medical appointments and do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
